extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reporting and writing news stories that reproduce speeches, interviews, and reports — focusing on accurate reproduction, appropriate condensation, and choices about format and human-interest treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: accurate reproduction of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: To reproduce as accurately as possible the ideas expressed by a speaker, by a person interviewed, or by the author of a report is obviously the only object in writing a news story dealing with such material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reporter's chief aim is fidelity to the original ideas; treat the utterance as the primary source. Avoid summarizing in ways that change meaning or emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid carelessness in taking down what is said
rubrics_metrics.description: Carelessness in taking down what is said is one of four common faults that endanger the accuracy of news stories of this type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reliable note-taking or stenographic methods; verify quotations when possible. Sloppy transcription leads directly to factual and interpretive errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid playing up statements taken from their context
rubrics_metrics.description: The playing up of statements that taken from their context are misleading is a common fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not lift striking phrases into a lead or highlight them in a way that misrepresents the speaker's actual thought or purpose; preserve contextual meaning when choosing highlights or pull-quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unintentional distortion through disproportionate emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Unintentional distortion due to giving disproportionate space or emphasis to some points is a danger in reporting speeches and reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance coverage of the main themes; ensure significant points receive proportional attention so the story doesn't convey a skewed impression of the original utterance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misrepresentation because of political partisanship or other bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Misrepresentation because of political partisanship or other bias is one of the four common faults; distortion and suppression of speeches, interviews, or reports because of political or other bias is indefensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain objectivity; do not omit or alter material to fit an agenda. Treat partisan pressures and editorializing as improper when they change the substance or spirit of the utterance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of quotation: substance, form, and spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: All quotation, direct or indirect, should be accurate not only in substance and form but also in spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify direct quotes for wording and tone; for indirect quotes preserve the speaker's intended meaning and overall tone. Beware that verbatim quotations can still mislead if isolated from context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensing, summarizing, and combining into a coherent whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Since news stories of this class must consist largely of direct and indirect quotation from an utterance, the problem ... is usually that of condensing, summarizing, and combining different parts of the available material into a unified, coherent whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skillfully select and reorder material to produce a clear narrative without altering meaning. Condensation must preserve logical connections and the speaker's main argument or narrative thread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray speaker and circumstances to stimulate reader interest
rubrics_metrics.description: In writing up interviews and speeches the reporter has a chance to portray clearly and attractively the speaker and the circumstances, thus stimulating the reader's interest in the utterance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use descriptive details about the speaker, audience, and setting to contextualize and engage readers — but do so sparingly so as not to overshadow the informational content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use human-interest elements in interviews when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: In interviews, on the other hand, it is possible to bring out the human interest element in portraying the character and personality of the person interviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage anecdotes, character details, and personal traits to add depth in interview pieces while ensuring these elements illuminate rather than distract from the subject's ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format choice: whether to include reporter's questions (Q&A vs. narrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter's questions, which are a necessary means of obtaining an expression of these ideas, are suppressed in many stories. In other stories, the questions are embodied in the answers or are repeated by the person interviewed. There is a growing tendency, particularly in signed stories of interviews, to give the reporter's questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide intentionally whether to present the interview as a Q&A or as a narrative/summarized account. Including questions can clarify context and make the exchange transparent (especially in signed pieces); suppressing them can produce smoother narrative flow.
